newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila protests over Chinese ships in dispute area.
newsitem.headline: Manila protests over Chinese ships in dispute area.

text.p: The Philippines said on Tuesday it was protesting to China after the intrusion of three Chinese naval frigates into an area claimed by Manila in the Spratly Islands.

The presidential palace said the Philippines was also informing its partners in the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) of the sighting of the vessels and the protest it was making to China.
"The Department of Foreign Affairs is sending a diplomatic protest to its counterpart in Beijing and will inform its ASEAN counterparts of these developments," the statement said.
The three vessels were spotted last Friday close to Kota and Panata islands in the Spratlys, a cluster of 190 potentially oil-rich but otherwise barren isles, shoals and reefs in the South China Sea.

The Spratly group is claimed wholly or in part by China, Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei. Manila's partners in ASEAN are Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

Armed forces chief General Arnulfo Acedera, in a report to President Fidel Ramos, said one of the vessels was identified as belonging to the Shuguang 04 Class and was accompanied by two small fishing boats and towing two other vessels.
A second vessel belonged to the Hai Class, it said.
"All the foreign naval vessels are of the frigate type, armed with deck guns," said the statement, which referred to three warships.

Philippine air force reconnaissance aircraft also discovered a new hut-like structure built over a reef six miles northeast of Kota island, it said. It did not say who built the structure or what it was used for.
Acedera has ordered the Western Command with responsibility over the islands claimed by Manila to carry out continuous surveillance of the area.

The Kota and Panata islands near which the supposed Chinese naval ships were sighted lie about halfway between Pagasa, the biggest island occupied by the Philippines in the Spratlys, and Mischief Reef, which Manila also claims but which the Chinese have occupied.
Tension flared between Manila and Beijing in 1995 when President Fidel Ramos accused the Chinese of building what he said looked like naval support structures on Mischief Reef.
Beijing said they were shelters for fishermen and has refused to dismantle them.
The Philippines has agreed on a code of conduct separately with China and Vietnam under which they agree to exercise self-restraint and not to use force in resolving the Spratlys row.
